name: Elymus

project_scope.selection_mode: Genus comparison lesson from live Master Plant Pool and existing Poaceae family module
project_scope.admission_note: Both taxa occur in the approved Master Plant Pool. This lesson does not install taxa or change settled range status.

shared_genus_characters.look_here_first: ELYMUS (wildryes) makes a continuous WHEATLIKE SPIKE with several-flowered SPIKELETS at nodes along the central RACHIS, not a loose branching PANICLE. To split the two installed species, inspect MATURE GLUME BASES: Canada often relatively straight/narrow V with DROOPING long-bristled heads; Virginia often hard, pale U-BOWED feet with ERECT more compact heads. Texas A&M cautions they hybridize, so conflicting characters stay Elymus sp.
shared_genus_characters.vegetative: Perennial cool-season grasses with jointed culms, leaf sheaths/blades and a ligule at the collar.
shared_genus_characters.reproductive: Inflorescence a terminal spike; spikelets sit along the rachis and contain multiple florets. Glumes and lemmas/awns carry the useful species characters.
shared_genus_characters.genus_confirmation: Node + sheath/collar/ligule confirms the grass doorway; a true terminal spike with multi-flowered spikelets along the rachis moves the learner into Elymus rather than the branched-panicle grasses.

species_comparison_matrix.look_first: Whole spike posture, then awns/glumes at one intact spikelet
species_comparison_matrix.architecture: Mature spikes commonly arch or nod conspicuously and have a long-bristly appearance from spreading/curving awns.
species_comparison_matrix.spikelet: Use the long conspicuous lemma awns and the glume/awn package as reproductive confirmation.
species_comparison_matrix.best_separator: A strongly nodding mature spike with long spreading/curving awns is the fast field door; confirm on an intact spikelet.
species_comparison_matrix.caution: Do not identify from 'nodding' alone—wind, maturity and damage change posture.

species_comparison_matrix.look_first: Whole spike posture, then glumes/awns at one intact spikelet
species_comparison_matrix.architecture: Spike is typically more erect/straight and visually tighter than Canada wildrye; awns are less dramatically spreading.
species_comparison_matrix.spikelet: Confirm with the comparatively compact spikelet/glume-awn architecture rather than leaf width or color.
species_comparison_matrix.best_separator: More erect compact spike + less dramatically spreading awns favors E. virginicus; reproductive close-up should confirm.
species_comparison_matrix.caution: Vegetative plants are unsafe for a forced species ID in this two-species lesson.

decision_sequence: Confirm Poaceae at a real culm node and collar/ligule.
Find a mature terminal spike and photograph the whole spike before zooming in.
Strongly nodding/arching, shaggy spike with long spreading/curving awns → E. canadensis door.
More erect/compact spike with less dramatically spreading awns → E. virginicus door.
Zoom to one intact spikelet and document glumes, florets and awns before finalizing.
If only leaves are present or the reproductive characters conflict, leave the plant at Elymus and route the observation to Taxonomy + Diagnostic Review.
overlap_and_cautions: Spike posture is a fast first split, not a stand-alone proof.
Leaf width, plant height, green color and habitat overlap and should remain supporting context only.
Broken or immature spikes can erase the strongest visual differences; require an intact mature reproductive unit for difficult plants.
Do not use generic 'wild rye' gestalt when spikelet structures are available.

realistic_lookalikes.separate_by: Compare the spikelet arrangement at each rachis node and the bristly awn architecture; photograph a node-level spikelet cluster rather than relying on the fuzzy silhouette.
Use an intact spikelet to document glumes, number of florets and awn origin; branched panicles exit the Elymus doorway immediately.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.purpose: Teach the quickest field split without relying on color.
Tie the fast silhouette cue to reproductive structure.
Teach what makes this a spike and separate look-alike spike grasses.
Reinforce the grass/genus workflow before species separation.
Prevent false confidence from overlapping leaves/habit.

media_routing.existing_project_media: Reuse exact Elymus project/user/Joey media only when it clearly shows one of the listed diagnostic roles.
media_routing.instruction: Highest-value acquisition is a matched mature-spike pair plus intact spikelet macros; generic meadow/habit photos are secondary.

diagnostic_review_handoffs: Verify difficult/intermediate Elymus material from an intact mature spikelet; do not force species from leaves alone.
Species taxonomy/range certification and canonical installation remain outside this lane.

genus_diagnostics.rachis: RACHIS is the central spike axis. Look at a node for attached multi-flowered spikelets, each with outer GLUMES and inner LEMMAS.
genus_diagnostics.glume_bases: On multiple ripe spikelets: pale outward bowing U of hardened outer glume feet supports VIRGINIA; straighter narrower V supports CANADA. The CC BY-SA Montana Virginia macro is source-reviewed and actually displays the U-shaped feet; do not assume all photos have enough detail. Hybrid intermediates cannot be forced.
genus_diagnostics.awns: The AWN is a bristle from a lemma. Canada wildrye often has long spreading or curving awns and a nodding spike; Virginia wildrye tends toward a tighter erect spike with shorter, straighter awns.
genus_diagnostics.collar: COLLAR is the blade/sheath junction; LIGULE is the small membrane inside. Useful grass anatomy, not a reliable species separator.

look_here_first: ELYMUS (wildryes) makes a continuous WHEATLIKE SPIKE with several-flowered SPIKELETS at nodes along the central RACHIS, not a loose branching PANICLE. To split the two installed species, inspect MATURE GLUME BASES: Canada often relatively straight/narrow V with DROOPING long-bristled heads; Virginia often hard, pale U-BOWED feet with ERECT more compact heads. Texas A&M cautions they hybridize, so conflicting characters stay Elymus sp.

comparison_lesson.title: Canada vs Virginia wildrye — true spike, glume bases and mature awns
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: CANADA: often long drooping spike and splayed awns; narrow V-like glume base. VIRGINIA: compact upright spike, paler bony U-like glume bases.
quick_split: Canada = mature spike generally arches or nods and has long spreading lemma awns. Base of outer glumes relatively slender/straight at central node.
Virginia = spike stays stiffer and upright, often compact; awns usually shorter/straighter; outer glume feet turn outward and harden pale/bony with U-like open base.
Both = cool-season perennial wildryes with MULTIFLOWERED spikelets attached at successive nodes on one central SPIKE; unlike Texas wintergrass's loose branching PANICLE.
Texas A&M notes hybridization between Canada and Virginia wildrye. Treat intermediate nodes/awns/posture as Elymus sp. unless voucher work resolves them.
comparison_lesson.field_safety: Cannot certify either species as target-zone native from this work; preserve UNRESOLVED range fields. Do not use vegetation-only or source image metadata to claim Hays specimen.

field_matrix.check: Always include entire attached mature spike.
Check many spikelets on one intact spike; overlap possible.

field_matrix.canada: Relatively straight and narrower, sharp V-type
field_matrix.check: Best anatomical comparison at 10–20× on multiple mature nodes.

field_matrix.canada: Two (sometimes more) multi-flowered spikelets along one central spike
field_matrix.virginia: Likewise multi-flowered spikelets at successive central nodes
field_matrix.check: Genus trait; not a species split.
Texas wintergrass has loose panicle of single-flowered spikelets.

visual_comparison.title: Elymus wildryes — real Canada awn/spikelet, flower, auricle and detached-bract lessons
visual_comparison.subtitle: Canada 9 Bob Harms source-original closeups now physically archived alongside five Virginia wildrye source originals and Canada vs Virginia structural comparison. Incomplete mm-level glume bases and local taxon vouchers remain flagged.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: ELYMUS: SPIKE not branched panicle; 2+ multi-FLORETED spikelets at rachis NODE; ligule a SHORT MEMBRANE, auricles = paired CLAWS. Canada (long awned mature nodding spikes, straighter narrow basal V glumes) vs Virginia (upright compact, thick outbowed U glume feet) but hybrids occur.

items.label: CANADA — two paired spikelets and narrow glumes at a rachis node
items.image_role: Original Montana macro shows pointed glumes and multiple florets, source-captioned as pairs at each central rachis joint
items.caption: Look for the central spike rachis and paired multiflowered spikelets. Long, narrow glumes flank their bases; leaflike bracts enclosing florets are lemmas. This source illustration is about GENUS architecture, not a pixel-proven V-shape glume-base measurement. Wikimedia's taxon depiction metadata is not fully consistent with the original source species label; use as source-labelled teaching reference.
items.why_it_matters: Explains what a spikelet, glume, rachis and lemma mean before the Canada versus Virginia distinction.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Original 1264×644 Commons photograph visibly inspected. Two gross structure arrows only; source describes glume/rachis group but not a botanically independently verified node-level taxon. Montana, not Hays.

items.label: CANADA — several mature arching/nodding spikes
items.image_role: Actual Montana landscape photo of multiple arching Canada wildrye heads; seedheads visible against dry roadcut
items.caption: Mature spikes arc and droop downward; the longer awns spread away from the spike axis. Look for the upper-left and mid-left bent spikes, not the unrelated plants in the background.
items.why_it_matters: Naturalistic growth form: several heads have obvious downward curves while the connected culms emerge from the clump.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: 960×720 Wikimedia source was visually inspected. Gross spike silhouettes arrowed; exact awn and glume-base anatomy not resolved from this wide scene.

items.label: VIRGINIA — actual pale, outward-bowed bony glume bases
items.image_role: Diagnostic Montana Matt Lavin high-contrast macro of two spikelets and four pale glumes with hardened divergent bases
items.caption: At the lowest part of the picture, each group of paired pale glumes bows away from the central point, creating a broad U or cup-shaped basal opening. The slender outer glumes flank hairy inner lemma/floret bodies. Compare Canada wildrye's typically narrower, straighter V-like glume bases, but allow intermediate hybrids.
items.why_it_matters: This is the species-level structure the existing Virginia gallery lacked; it is much stronger than an upright-head silhouette alone.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: Actual 544×1344 Wikimedia file visually inspected at native aspect ratio; lower bowed/bony bases and paired outer glumes are legible, arrows only to gross photographed structures. Original photographer specifically identifies this feature; no local Hays morphology claimed.

items.label: VIRGINIA — upright compact flowering spikes
items.image_role: Montana source-labelled Virginia wildrye photograph, three erect crowded wheatlike mature heads with short straighter awns
items.caption: Three stiffly ascending seed spikes with closely packed awned spikelets. Their posture and compactness support Virginia compared to the looser Canada mature head; photographed spikelets alone are not enough if hybridization is suspected.
items.why_it_matters: Shows the upright compact seedhead silhouette as the first field decision.
items.creator: Matt Lavin
items.photo_status: 500×667 Commons image inspected. Gross seedhead and spikelet grouping arrowed, NOT glume-base anatomy; original source Montana.

items.label: TEXAS WINTERGRASS — loose PANICLE, one long awn per hard floret (comparison only)
items.image_role: USDA-ARS public-domain mature fruit; different grass genus with open panicle not a crowded multiflowered spike
items.caption: One very long twisted awn emerges from one hard sharply pointed fertile lemma; Elymus has a central spike axis with multiple florets within spikelets at successive nodes. Compare the whole flowering head before counting awns.
items.why_it_matters: Prevents confusion between two cool-season Texas native-looking grasses by distinguishing a true spike and an open panicle.
items.creator: Tracey Slotta / USDA-ARS
items.photo_status: USDA-PD source previously verified and annotated on original wintergrass card; comparison-only with no reused incorrect coordinate markers.
